1. Sources, prerequisites, and chapter scope

The four core written courses are MIT 6.046J, CMU 15-451/651, Princeton COS423 and Stanford CS166. ETH Zurich supplies an additional reviewed comparison. The linked source audit records complete reading ranges, instructor verification, inaccessible candidates and corrections. Sources agree on the central idea but sometimes use different primitive costs or resize timing; those differences matter when a question asks for an exact number.

Prerequisites are geometric series, binary representation, asymptotic notation, stacks, queues, arrays and elementary induction. This chapter develops a method for every legal operation sequence, including adversarial sequences. It extends earlier array and heap chapters by deriving proof coefficients, endpoint terms, hysteresis conditions and failure examples. It does not certify every unseen examination question.

2. What is being bounded?

Let D0 be the initial data-structure state. Operation i transforms Di-1 into Di and costs ci≥0 measured in specified primitives. The sequence length N counts public operations, not the number of elements currently stored. A statement that total cost is at most aN+b means the same constants work for every legal sequence from the permitted initial state. The expensive operation can occur anywhere that the state permits it.

In the laboratory, T denotes cumulative real work and A denotes cumulative amortized charges. The displayed endpoint formula T=A+Φ0-ΦN is evaluated only when the current public operation is complete. Storage positions are numbered; labels beginning with K identify records and labels beginning with I identify original input indices. These identifiers follow objects even when their storage positions change.

Worst-case time for one operation maximizes that operation's cost over reachable states. Amortized time bounds a complete sequence by relating its operations. Average-case time averages over a distribution on inputs. Expected time averages over specified random choices. These are different quantifiers. A deterministic two-stack queue has constant amortized time without any assumption that inputs are random; a randomized hash table can instead have expected amortized time.

The phrase constant amortized cost does not mean constant response time. If an append copies a million records, that particular append remains expensive even when earlier cheap appends pay for it in a proof. Throughput and latency answer different questions.

3. Aggregate analysis and prefix validity

Aggregate analysis directly bounds the sum of real costs. If each of P inserted records can be removed at most once, total removals are at most P even when one call removes many records. Charging every call its largest individually possible cost loses this dependency.

The bound must hold for every prefix that the theorem allows. A future operation cannot retrospectively rescue an earlier prefix whose required upper bound has already failed. For an initially empty stack with push cost one and removal cost one, total element work is at most 2P≤2N. If every public call also costs one for dispatch/checking, add N. Empty multipop calls then have cost one rather than zero. State the chosen model before quoting an exact charge.

4. Accounting: where credits live

Assign a charge ai to each operation and maintain balance Bi=Bi-1+ai-ci. If B0=0 and every prefix has Bi≥0, then actual total is no larger than total charges. A proof must specify what carries the credits and which event consumes them. For a stack, charge two for a push: one pays for insertion and one stays with that record until removal. A record cannot spend the same credit twice.

For a structure that starts nonempty, unused removal credits must be supplied initially or the final bound must include the starting workload. Saying that the credits are on the records is insufficient if those records were never charged in the analyzed sequence. When comparing different operations, different charges are allowed; a queue need not charge enqueue and dequeue equally.

5. Potential: the full telescoping theorem

Choose a real-valued state function Φ. Define the amortized charge by

c^i=ci+Φ(Di)-Φ(Di-1).

Summing cancels every internal endpoint, leaving the exact identity

∑i=1Nci=∑i=1Nc^i+Φ(D0)-Φ(DN).

If every reachable endpoint satisfies Φ(DN)≥Φ(D0), the charge sum directly upper-bounds actual work. The common sufficient condition Φ(D0)=0 and Φ≥0 is convenient but not logically necessary. If only Φ≥0 is known and the initial potential is positive, keep the additive Φ(D0) term. More generally, a known lower bound L gives total work at most the charge sum plus Φ(D0)-L.

An individual charge can be negative: that means an operation releases more stored credit than its actual cost. It is not a negative running time. Adding the same constant to all potentials does not change any charge or endpoint difference. Multiplying a potential by a constant changes charges and is useful when one move costs several primitive units.

6. Deriving a potential rather than guessing

A useful potential increases during cheap preparation and drops during expensive cleanup. Begin with the exact expensive transition. Suppose cleanup costs qm and changes a candidate state measure by -m. Multiply that measure by at least q to pay for the cleanup. Then check every cheap transition and every reachable boundary.

For doubling arrays, free slots alone point in the wrong direction: a full array has zero free slots, then growth creates many free slots while also costing much. The potential rises when it should pay out. The expression 2n-C instead accumulates as a capacity- C array fills. Clipping it at zero handles the initially sparse states.

Never cancel O(m) against -O(m) without choosing a concrete coefficient or a known upper-bound coefficient. The two hidden constants need not match. Potential design is an inequality problem with a cost contract, not symbolic cancellation of asymptotic labels.

7. Multipop stacks and initial workload

Our stack supports push, pop-if-nonempty, and multipop( k), which removes min(k,n) elements for nonnegative integer k. In the element-only model, push costs one and a multipop that removes r elements costs r. Take Φ=n. A push has charge two; each removal has charge zero because r units of potential pay r units of work. With a constant call overhead, add that overhead to each charge.

A stack starting with s records has initial potential s. Total element work is at most 2P+s for the analyzed pushes and removals. The additive term cannot be discarded when s is an independent input parameter: one multipop can consume all s initial records. A multipush( k) that creates k records must cost and be charged proportional to k; a constant bound per public call would be false.

8. Binary counters: exact counts and overflow

For an unbounded nonnegative binary counter, increment clears its t trailing one bits and sets the next zero. Actual bit flips are t+1. The potential is the number of one bits, so its change is 1-t and every increment has charge two. Starting from zero after N increments, the exact total is

F(N)=∑j≥0⌊N2j⌋=2N-popcount(N).

To prove the second equality, write N=∑jbj2j. Each set bit contributes 2j+1-1 to the floor sum; summing gives twice the value minus the number of set bits. The first increment has one flip, not two; the unused one unit is the final potential.

For a width- w counter that wraps modulo 2w, only bits 0 through w-1 exist. Starting at zero, the exact count for any N is ∑j=0w-1⌊N/2j⌋. On an all-ones wrap, cost is w, potential drops by w, and charge is zero. For a nonzero initial state, retain its popcount as an additive term. If increment and decrement alternate around a carry boundary, every operation can flip w bits; increment-only amortization does not prove constant cost for this enlarged operation set.

9. Dynamic arrays: exact geometric copying

Consider an initially empty array of capacity one. Append doubles capacity only when the old array is full, copies all live records, then writes the new record. One record copy and one new-record write each cost one; allocation and index checks are excluded from this exact model. After N≥1 appends, let C=2⌈log2N⌉, with C=1 for N=1. Copied capacities are 1,2,…,C/2, totaling C-1. Hence exact work is

T(N)=N+C-1<3N.

At N=8, no capacity-eight copy occurs: the array only becomes full. At N=9, that copy occurs and capacity becomes sixteen. This strict boundary is a frequent source of off-by-one answers. The number of expansions is ⌈log2N⌉ for positive N, and zero for N=0.

The theorem covers appending, not arbitrary position insertion. Front insertion shifts all existing elements; N such operations cause N(N-1)/2 shifts regardless of how well resizing is amortized. The real operation cost includes both shifting and rebuilding.

10. Insert-only potential and general growth factors

Use Φ(n,C)=max(0,2n-C). Initially it is zero. Without growth, the potential increase is at most two and actual cost is one, giving charge at most three. When old n=C and the new state is (C+1,2C), potential changes from C to two. Actual work is C+1, so the charge is exactly three, including the capacity-one boundary.

For ideal exact capacity multiplication by fixed r>1, use

Φ(n,C)=max(0,rn-Cr-1).

A full table has potential C; after copying into capacity rC and appending, potential is r/(r-1). Both growing and ordinary appends have charge at most 1+r/(r-1). If integer capacities use C'=⌈rC⌉, the growth potential decreases at least as much when the new-state expression stays positive; if clipping occurs, the old C potential still pays all copies, leaving charge one. Therefore the same upper bound works. It is an upper bound, not an exact identical charge after rounding.

As r approaches one, the constant grows. Constant additive growth C'=C+d instead copies an arithmetic series and produces quadratic total work for fixed d. Choosing r=1+1/N for a workload of length N does not give a uniform constant bound; the parameter itself changes with the input.

11. Weighted primitives and allocation

If an ordinary append costs u and moving an old record costs v, scale the insert-only potential by v. Charges are at most u+vr/(r-1) under the reduced model. If allocating or clearing a new capacity- rC buffer costs arC, the rebuild coefficient becomes v+ar per old record. A potential scaled by that coefficient proves constant amortized cost for fixed a,v,r, but the numerical charge is larger.

Record moves can themselves be nonconstant. Copying a string of length L is not a unit record move unless the array stores fixed-size handles. User-defined constructors, destructors, allocation failure and exception rollback require separate contracts. Pointer/reference invalidation affects correctness even when operation counts remain favorable. A time theorem does not automatically imply a safe client API.

12. Why naive halving thrashes

Starting from n=C/2+1 in a capacity- C table, a deletion to C/2 followed by immediate halving leaves the smaller table full. The next insertion doubles it again. Alternate these operations near the boundary and pay proportional to C almost every time. The cheap preparatory work that growth requires has been undone by shrinking too early.

The remedy is hysteresis: use distinct grow and shrink thresholds. Doubling at full occupancy and halving at one-quarter occupancy leaves the resized array near half occupancy. Reaching either trigger again requires a linear number of intervening operations in the current capacity. A picture of spare space is not enough; derive the number of required inserts or deletions.

13. Quarter-full shrinking: complete case analysis

The main policy uses capacity powers of two with minimum capacity two. Append grows before writing if full. Pop removes the last record first, then halves when C>2 and the new size is at most C/4. Empty pop returns no record and costs a constant check. In legal states reached from the empty minimum-capacity table, a shrink event crosses the threshold from C/4+1 to exactly C/4.

For completed states choose

For dense states with n≥C/2, define Φ(n,C)=2n-C. For sparse states with n<C/2, define Φ(n,C)=C/2-n. At the shared boundary both expressions equal zero, so the definition is continuous there.

It is nonnegative. Initially Φ(0,2)=1, so keep a plus-one endpoint allowance. A normal append in the high branch has charge three; in the low branch it has charge zero, with the crossing into exact half occupancy also costing zero. A growth has charge three. A normal nonempty pop in the high branch has charge minus one, except crossing from half occupancy into the low branch has charge two. A low-branch pop without shrink has charge two.

For a shrink with old capacity C≥8, old size C/4+1 has potential C/4-1. The new size is C/4, new capacity C/2 and final potential zero. Cost is 1+C/4, so charge is two. At C=4, the crossing begins at half occupancy and old potential zero; the new state (1,2) also has potential zero, so charge is two again. Empty pops have charge one in the check-only model. Thus every append has charge at most three and every pop at most two, and total work is at most 3P+2Q+1 for P appends and Q pops.

def pop_last(a, size, capacity):
    if size == 0:
        return a, size, capacity, None
    value = a[size - 1]
    size -= 1
    if capacity > 2 and size <= capacity // 4:
        capacity //= 2
        a = copy_live_records(a, size, capacity)
    return a, size, capacity, value

If a course checks occupancy before deletion, compute that transition separately. At old size C/4, it copies C/4 records first and then removes one. Its endpoint has size C/4-1 and capacity C/2, giving potential one rather than zero. The asymptotic theorem survives, but an exact charge copied from the post-delete proof does not.

14. General hysteresis and space bounds

Suppose growth multiplies capacity by r>1 at full occupancy and shrink divides capacity by r when occupancy reaches β. Immediately after growth, occupancy is approximately 1/r; immediately after shrink, it is approximately rβ. A fixed strict condition 0<β<1/r separates both new states from the opposite trigger. The distances 1/r-β and 1-rβ must be bounded away from zero independently of input size for uniform constants.

In the doubling/quarter policy, a nonempty completed table has capacity at most max(2,4n) and at least n. Empty storage is bounded by the minimum capacity. During rebuilding, old and new buffers coexist; peak storage is larger than the capacity of either one alone. A spatial theorem must distinguish steady-state and transient storage.

15. Two-stack queues: order and exact charge

Maintain an input stack and output stack. Enqueue pushes onto input. Dequeue pops output if it is nonempty; otherwise it transfers every input record by one input pop and one output push, then pops output. The logical FIFO order is output from top to bottom followed by input from bottom to top. This order invariant remains true after a complete transfer.

Count each primitive push or pop as one. Set Φ=2|input|. Enqueue costs one and adds two potential units, so charge is three. Dequeue without transfer costs one and does not change potential, so charge is one. Transferring k records and then removing one costs 2k+1, drops potential by 2k, and also has charge one. Empty checks can be added explicitly. Starting from empty, total primitive work is at most three times enqueues plus nonempty dequeues.

A front/peek operation can trigger a transfer but omit the final output pop; its transfer charge is zero under the primitive-only model. Repeated peeks do not repeatedly transfer. If an implementation transfers when output is already nonempty, newer items can be put ahead of older ones and break FIFO correctness.

16. Monotonic stacks and nested loops

For each incoming value, remove stack-top values that are smaller than it, then push its index. Although an inner loop can run many times for one input, every index is pushed once and popped at most once. Total stack modifications are at most 2N. Each successful comparison causes a pop; at most one final failed comparison occurs per incoming element. Hence comparisons are at most 2N-1 for a nonempty input when only comparisons between actual values are counted.

Equality is part of the specification. Pop while top is strictly smaller when equal values must remain; pop while top is smaller or equal when a later equal value supersedes an earlier candidate. Nearest greater, nearest greater-or-equal and sliding-window maximum are different queries. For window algorithms, expired indices are removed separately and still at most once. State the invariant during processing and the final answer direction before drawing the stack.

17. Binary carries, sorted blocks and binomial links

Represent a growing collection by at most one sorted block of each size 2j. Insert a singleton and merge equal-sized blocks exactly as a binary increment carries. A merge producing a block of size 2j costs proportional to 2j. During N insertions, that level is built ⌊N/2j⌋ times, so each level contributes at most N work and all levels together give O(NlogN) total. The amortized insertion is logarithmic, despite a linear worst-case carry.

To search, binary-search every occupied block. At size N, search cost is O(∑j:bj=1(j+1)), which can be quadratic in logN when every low bit is set. This is not the same cost as linking binomial trees: an equal-rank tree link is constant work, so root-count potential can give constant amortized insertion for a maintained forest. Treating a sorted-array merge as a constant link silently changes the algorithm.

18. Advanced extensions and honest boundaries

For sorted insertion into a B-tree, a pointer to the rightmost leaf avoids repeated root-to-leaf searches. Expensive splits occur after enough keys accumulated at that level. Summing split counts across levels gives linear construction work for fixed branching rules and constant-size primitive metadata. If the branching factor is an input parameter, charge key moves and pointer updates explicitly; a right-spine key potential needs root-boundary terms. The source shorthand about nodes and keys is not used as a complete proof here.

Move-to-front illustrates a different use of potential: comparing one algorithm with a competing algorithm. Count inversions between their list orders. Accessing an item at position p removes inversions involving items after it in the competitor and creates inversions involving preceding items. Under the specified list-update model, this yields a competitive bound proportional to the competitor's total cost. It does not make every list access constant time; repeatedly accessing the current last item can remain linear per access. Competitiveness is a relative guarantee, amortized complexity is an absolute sequence bound.

Sparse-set initialization stores active indices in a dense list and checks a reverse pointer before trusting a cell. A reset can clear the logical active length without clearing every possible cell. In a word-RAM model with arbitrary readable words, initialization work can be independent of the universe size; in a language that prohibits reading uninitialized memory, use initialized metadata, epochs or a different memory contract. Epoch counters require a wrap policy. This technique is a representation argument, not permission to invoke undefined behavior.

19. Expected amortization, persistence and deamortization

If rebuilding a hash table scans every old record, geometric resizing bounds the number of rebuild record visits deterministically. If each reinsertion has expected constant collision cost under a stated hash family and load bound, expected total rebuild work is linear. A deterministic geometric-series proof alone does not prove deterministic constant dictionary operations. Adaptive adversaries and reused randomness may invalidate a probabilistic assumption; state the model.

In a persistent structure, two branches can both request the same deferred cleanup from a shared old state. A potential that pays for one cleanup cannot be spent on both branches without recharging or memoizing shared work. A linear history proof does not automatically prove a tree of histories.

Deamortization spreads cleanup over subsequent operations. To grow capacity C to 2C, begin copying at the overflow event and copy at least one old record per following append, with a schedule that finishes before the new buffer fills. Reads must route to the old or new location according to a migration boundary, and writes must update the authoritative location. Constant allocation of the new buffer is a separate assumption. Concurrent mutations, deletions, iterator validity and copy failures are additional requirements; merely limiting copy count does not prove an entire production API has constant worst-case latency.

20. A procedure for formula and conceptual examination questions

First identify the sequence length, the current number of records and the initial state separately. Second identify the exact charged primitive and the permitted operations. Third compute the expensive transition, including whether resize occurs before or after the update. Fourth choose aggregate, accounting or potential reasoning that captures a resource consumed only once. Fifth retain the initial and final potential terms. Finally test the smallest capacity, an exact power-of-two endpoint, an empty operation and an adversarial alternating sequence.

For multiple-choice questions, eliminate statements whose quantifiers differ: amortized is not expected, per-operation worst case is not sequence worst case, a bound for appends is not a bound for shifts, and a result from empty is not a result from an arbitrarily full initial buffer. The problem bank develops these distinctions through complete algebra, numerical traces and counterexamples.

21. Complete-sentence chapter summary

Amortized analysis bounds every permitted operation sequence by tracking preparation and cleanup across time. Aggregate analysis sums work directly; accounting keeps a prefix-solvent balance; potential analysis expresses the same resource through a state function and an exact telescoping identity. Initial workload and the endpoint potential determine whether a charge sum alone bounds real work.

Increment-only counters, bounded multipop stacks and correctly implemented two-stack queues admit constant amortized operation costs in their declared primitive models. Geometric array growth copies a geometric series, while additive growth copies an arithmetic series. Growth and shrinking require distinct thresholds to avoid repeated rebuilds. Weighted moves, allocation, arbitrary-position shifts, enlarged operation sets and persistent branching can change the guarantee. Deamortization adds scheduling and representation obligations that amortization alone does not satisfy.

Authenticated MSc and doctoral examination bridges

Question 1. Constant-time maximum with restoration

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

Phd CE 1404 · Q9 · PDF page 4. Revisited original examination bridge; independently derived answer, not an official key.

A stack S supports PUSH, POP and TOP. Design FIND-MAX(S) to return the largest currently stored value efficiently. Which proposed approach is correct and efficient?

1.

Maintain one MAX variable on PUSH. FIND-MAX is constant time, but rebuilding MAX after a POP needs linear time.

2.

Each FIND-MAX pops all elements, computes the maximum, and restores the original order. Each query is linear.

3.

On every PUSH, an auxiliary stack M stores the maximum of the prefix then present in S. A POP also removes M's top. FIND-MAX is constant time.

4.

On every PUSH, recursively compute the maximum of the current stack and append it to S. FIND-MAX takes logarithmic time.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 3.

Option 3 stores one cached maximum per data-stack prefix. Induction proves each M entry is the maximum of the corresponding S prefix; synchronous POP exposes the prior valid prefix. PUSH, POP, TOP of M and FIND-MAX all use constant operations, and M uses O(n) space. Duplicates are retained because every push stores a prefix result. Option 1 explicitly needs a linear rebuild after removing the current maximum, so it does not give the same complete efficient interface. Option 2 preserves the answer and order only with restoration storage but scans on every query. Option 4 adds metadata as if it were data and gives no valid logarithmic recurrence. Empty-stack maximum must have a specified error/identity policy. This is an independently derived answer, not an official key.

Amortization test. Repeated FIND-MAX calls that pop and restore the same n records each cost linear time: restoration recreates the work rather than consuming it permanently. N such calls cost Theta(Nn). The prefix-max metadata construction instead gives constant worst-case calls; it does not rely on amortizing repeated full scans.

Question 2. Sequential merge versus a heap-head frontier

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MS CE 1405 · Q56 · PDF page 12. Revisited original examination bridge; independently derived answer, not an official key.

There are k sorted lists, each containing n/k elements. Merge lists 1 and 2, then merge the result with list 3, and continue in this way. What is the worst-case running-time bound of this algorithm?

1.
O(klogn)
2.
O(n)
3.
O(nlogk)
4.
O(nk)
Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

  1. At stage j, merge an accumulated list of jn/k elements with the next list of n/k elements. In the standard linear-time merge model, the worst-case work is proportional to (j+1)n/k.
  2. Sum the stage costs for j=1,…,k-1: (n/k)(2+3+…+k)=(n/k)(k(k+1)/2-1). For 2≤k≤n, this is Θ(nk), so option 4 is the stated bound.
  3. A balanced merge tree instead processes all n elements at each of Θ(logk) levels and takes Θ(nlogk). A heap can achieve the same asymptotic bound, but neither is the sequential algorithm in the question.
  4. The worst case includes inputs whose keys remain interleaved at successive merges; one cannot price every stage at the size of the incoming list alone. If k is fixed independently of n, the expression becomes linear in n, but the listed options treat both parameters as variable.

Transfer rule. Write the accumulated problem size at each iteration before summing costs. A correct bound for a different merge strategy is a distractor, not an answer.

Amortization test. Sequential accumulation revisits old elements in many later merges, creating an arithmetic sum. Binary-level rebuilding lets each record participate only once per level, creating logarithmic amortized insertion. The different total bounds follow from different lifetime participation counts, not the word merge alone.

Original and reconstructed formula/concept problems

Question 3. Telescoping with both endpoints

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A six-operation sequence has charges summing to 31, initial potential 9 and final potential 14. Find actual work. Is 31 an upper bound?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Expand each charge as actual cost plus its potential change. Internal changes cancel, so actual work is 31+9-14=26. The charge sum exceeds actual work by five because the final state retains five more credit units than the initial state. Thus 31 is an upper bound for this endpoint. This calculation alone does not prove the bound for all other reachable endpoints; that requires a lower bound relative to the initial potential.

Question 4. A nonzero initial state invalidates a claim

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A proposed proof has charges at most four per operation and nonnegative potential. It starts at potential 50. What bound is justified for N operations, and why is 4N unsupported?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Telescoping gives T≤4N+50-ΦN≤4N+50. Nonnegativity only implies that final potential is at least zero, not at least 50. An operation can consume initially stored work. For example, one multipop on 50 preloaded stack records costs 50 in a removal-only model while dropping potential by 50. The omitted initial term is precisely what would pay for it.

Question 5. Negative charges do not mean negative time

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

An operation costs 7 and changes potential from 20 to 9. Compute its charge and explain whether the proof is invalid.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The charge is 7+9-20=-4. Actual work remains seven. Eleven stored units were released, seven paid for work and four reduce the total charge account. This is legal if the chosen endpoint lower bound still holds for the full sequence. Requiring every charge to be nonnegative is an optional accounting convention, not a requirement of the telescoping identity.

The constant shift cancels in every difference: (Φi+100)-(Φi-1+100)=Φi-Φi-1. It also cancels between initial and final endpoints, so it cannot repair a false relative endpoint argument. Scaling triples the difference and can change charges. Its initial allowance and lower bound must also be scaled. A shift changes the displayed zero level; a scale changes the amount of stored credit.

Enqueue 1,2,3; dequeue once; enqueue 4,5; dequeue three times. Give output order and exact stack work.

Returns are 1,2,3,4. The first transfer moves three records, costing six; after old output empties, the later transfer moves two, costing four. Five enqueues cost five and four returned output pops cost four, so total is nineteen. Final input is empty and output contains 5; charges 15+4=19 agree. Transferring newer records while older output remains would change the order.

Question 52. Peek-triggered transfer

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

After six enqueues, issue ten front queries and no dequeues. Each front performs a transfer only if output is empty. Count primitive pushes/pops.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Six enqueues cost six. The first front transfers six records with twelve primitive stack operations. Subsequent fronts read the same output top without stack modification, so primitive work is eighteen. The six enqueues were charged eighteen; the transfer releases twelve potential units and has zero primitive-only charge. Include ten query-check/read units if those are part of the cost model.

Question 53. Why queue-size potential is wrong

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Try potential equal to total queue size for a transfer-triggered dequeue with k input records. Compute its charge.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Queue size decreases only by one although the transfer costs 2k stack primitives. The dequeue cost is 2k+1 and potential change minus one, giving charge 2k. Thus this potential does not prove a constant charge. The correct measure counts pending input-to-output work, so twice input-stack size drops by 2k.

Question 54. Weighted two-stack transfer

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Input pop costs two, output push costs three, and output pop costs four. Input push costs one. Choose potential and charges.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each pending input record requires five units to migrate, so choose Φ=5|input|. Enqueue charge is six. Transfer-triggered dequeue costs 5k+4 and drops potential by 5k, so charge four. A normal output dequeue also costs four. This derivation chooses the coefficient from the actual migration primitives rather than assuming a universal coefficient two.

Question 55. A preloaded input stack

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A queue begins with twenty records on input and none on output. Bound one dequeue and explain the initial credit.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Transfer costs forty and the returned pop one, so actual work is 41. The operation’s charge under 2|input| is one, but initial potential is forty and final potential zero. The endpoint identity restores actual cost 41. A theorem from empty cannot be applied to this state while omitting initial preparation.

Question 56. A monotonic stack numerical trace

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Process [3,1,4,2,5], popping while the old top is strictly smaller than the incoming value. Count pushes, pops and actual value comparisons.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Push 3; 1 compares unsuccessfully with 3. Value 4 pops 1 and 3. Value 2 compares unsuccessfully with 4. Value 5 pops 2 and 4. There are five pushes, four pops and six comparisons: two failures plus four successes. Final stack contains index four/value five. The nested loop is linear in total because each index leaves at most once.

Question 57. Equality changes the query

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Process [4,4,4] using strict-smaller and smaller-or-equal pop rules. Compare final stacks and pop counts.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

With strict-smaller, every equality test fails, no record is popped and all three indices remain. With smaller-or-equal, the prior equal index is popped before each later push, giving two pops and only the last index remaining. Both have linear total work. They encode different tie contracts, so the faster-looking drawing is not a substitute for specifying the requested query.

Question 58. A comparison upper bound

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

For N incoming values, prove at most 2N-1 comparisons between actual stack values in the standard monotonic algorithm.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each successful comparison pops a previously pushed index, so at most N-1 successes occur: the final inserted index has not been popped during the loop. Each input after the first can have at most one failed comparison, so failures are at most N-1. This gives the sharper bound 2N-2 for N at least two, hence the claimed 2N-1 also holds. Empty-stack checks are separate and should not be included as value comparisons.

Question 59. Sliding-window expiration

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A monotonic deque removes indices from its front when they leave a window and from its back when dominated. Can an index be charged twice for removal?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. Once an index leaves the deque by either route, it cannot later be removed from that same deque again. Every index is inserted once and removed at most once, so total modifications are linear. Expiration comparisons and one final failed dominance test per input add only linear overhead. Correctness also requires indices, not values alone, to distinguish equal values at different ages.

Question 60. Sorted-block insertion exact writes

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Insert eight singleton records into the binary sorted-block method. Charge one for each singleton write and the output length for each merge. Find total writes.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Level-one blocks of size two are produced four times, costing eight writes; size-four blocks twice, costing eight; size-eight once, costing eight. Singleton writes cost eight. Total is 32. A single eighth insertion costs fifteen writes across singleton plus 2+4+8 merge outputs, but total eight-insertion work is logarithmic per insertion on average.

Question 61. Sorted-block search at all-one size

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

At N=31, occupied block sizes are 1,2,4,8,16. Bound the sum of binary-search comparison budgets using j+1 for a size- 2j block.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The budgets are one through five, totaling fifteen. In general N=2h-1 occupies levels zero through h-1, totaling h(h+1)/2=Θ(h2). Binary search in each block does not make the combined search logarithmic when a logarithmic number of increasingly large blocks must be visited.

Question 62. A carry with unit links instead of merges

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Insert a singleton into a canonical binomial forest of size 31. Count links, actual normalized work and root-count charge.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Size 31 has ranks zero through four. The new singleton carries through five equal-rank links and leaves one rank-five tree. With one unit for initial insertion plus each link, actual cost is six. Root count changes from five to one, dropping four, so charge is two. Sorted-array merging at these levels would instead move 2+4+8+16+32 records and is a different primitive model.

Question 63. Total binary carries

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

How many equal-rank links occur while inserting N singleton trees into an empty canonical binomial forest?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Begin with N singleton roots created over the sequence. Each link reduces root count by exactly one. Final root count is popcount(N), so total links are N-popcount(N). This telescoping argument is independent of which key becomes parent, provided canonical equal-rank linking is maintained.

Question 64. Different merge cost at each level

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A binary-block rebuilding algorithm spends 22j when constructing a block of size 2j. Bound total cost for N=2h.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Level j is constructed N/2j times, costing N2j at that level. Sum from j=1 through h to get N(2h+1-2)=Θ(N2). The logarithmic amortized insertion theorem depended on linear rebuild cost in block length; quadratic rebuilding changes the result.

Question 65. Right-spine B-tree assumptions

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Why does a pointer to the rightmost leaf matter when building a B-tree from sorted keys, and why must root split work be handled?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Every next key belongs at the rightmost leaf, so the pointer avoids a fresh root-to-leaf search for each insertion. Splits can still propagate upward and must be charged to keys accumulated at their levels. A new root may add right-spine metadata rather than simply reducing it, so a potential proof must include that boundary. Fixed branching factor simplifies constants; variable branching factor and key moves require explicit accounting.

Question 66. Move-to-front is not constant access

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

For a list of n distinct keys, always access the current last key and move it to the front. What is the total access cost for N requests?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Every access examines position n under the position-cost model, so total is Nn. Move-to-front’s competitive guarantee compares its cost with another permitted list-update algorithm on the same request sequence. It does not say every access sequence has linear cost in the number of requests alone. Relative and absolute guarantees must not be interchanged.

Question 67. Sparse-set membership guard

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A sparse representation uses dense[0..k-1] and a reverse position s[x]. State the guard that prevents an old reverse value from falsely claiming membership after reset.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

First require 0≤s[x]<k, then require dense[s[x]] equals x. The second check verifies the round trip; the first prevents reading outside the active dense prefix. Reset sets k to zero, making every membership test fail regardless of stale reverse entries. In a language requiring initialized reverse cells, supply initialized metadata or a valid epoch representation before reading s[x].

Question 68. Epoch counter wrap

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A reset-based dictionary uses a width-eight epoch and stores each key’s last epoch. What failure occurs after 256 resets without clearing metadata?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The current epoch repeats modulo 256. A stale entry tagged with that same old epoch can now be mistaken for active even though it was not inserted in the current cycle. Use a wider nonwrapping contract, explicitly clear tags at wrap, or maintain additional disambiguation. Rare clearing has to be analyzed in the operation cost; it cannot be ignored as impossible when the epoch is finite.

Question 69. Expected rebuild work

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

An array-backed hash dictionary doubles. Rebuild visits are geometrically bounded, but reinserting each key has expected constant cost. What bound is justified?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The number of visited records across growth is deterministically linear in the inserted-record prefix. If the stated random-hash assumptions guarantee a uniform expected bound for each reinsertion, linearity of expectation gives expected linear rebuilding time. It does not give a deterministic linear bound on collision processing. Independence of all individual costs is unnecessary for linearity, but the conditional model must remain valid.

Question 70. An adversary and recycled randomness

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Why may an expected collision estimate become invalid when an adaptive adversary observes a fixed hash function and chooses new keys?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The original estimate may apply to keys fixed independently of the random function. After observing placements, an adversary can choose keys concentrated in a known bucket. The operation sequence then depends on the randomness, changing the quantifiers. A fresh or stronger randomized model, adversary restriction or deterministic worst-case dictionary is needed to justify the bound.

Question 71. Persistent branching spends credit twice

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A persistent two-stack queue has k input records and no output. Two independent branches each dequeue from that shared state without memoizing the transfer. Count work.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each branch performs its own k-record transfer plus one removal, costing 2k+1. Combined work is 4k+2. The old state’s 2k potential can pay for one transfer along one history, but cannot automatically pay twice across a branching history. Memoized shared reversal or branch-specific recharging is required for a corresponding total-history bound.

Question 72. Migration budget before capacity exhaustion

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

An append-only array doubles from C to 2C at overflow. If one old record is copied on the overflow append and each subsequent append, when does copying finish?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There are C old records, so C scheduled appends including the triggering append complete the copy. Starting at size C, after these appends the size is 2C, just filling the new buffer. Copying finishes before a later append would trigger the next growth. This count assumes each scheduled copy and new write is constant time and the new buffer allocation is available without linear latency.

Question 73. Routing reads during migration

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Old buffer capacity is eight, new capacity sixteen, and the first three old indices have migrated. Where should a read of indices two, five and ten go?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Index two is below the migration boundary and should use the new buffer. Index five is still in the old live prefix and should use the old buffer. Index ten is a newly appended position and exists only in the new buffer. A representation invariant must also route writes consistently; blindly reading every index from new storage sees uninitialized old records.

Question 74. Allocation blocks a latency claim

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

An incremental copier moves one record per append, but allocation zero-fills the whole new buffer synchronously. Is append worst-case constant?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. The triggering append still pays linear work to allocate or zero the new buffer. Incremental record copying only bounds one component of the operation. A constant-latency theorem requires an allocator/virtual-memory contract or an additional incremental initialization scheme that respects legal reads and writes.

Question 75. An arbitrary subinterval of a cheap-charge history

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A valid potential proof starts at zero. Does every subinterval have real work bounded by its own charge sum?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Not necessarily. For an interval from s+1 through t, actual work is its charge sum plus Φs-Φt. A subinterval beginning with high stored credit can consume it, so its actual work can exceed charges. The whole-prefix theorem from the initial zero state remains valid. A full array’s next append is the simplest illustration.

Question 76. Repeated rebuilding without state growth

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

An operation reconstructs an unchanged n-record array on every call. Can a potential of array size prove constant amortized time?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Every call costs proportional to n while the state size is unchanged, so potential difference is zero and charge remains proportional to n. Repeating N calls costs Nn. Amortization needs a resource that actually accumulates and is consumed; attaching a plausible-looking potential to an unchanged state cannot manufacture a faster bound.

Question 77. A history-dependent account as an augmented state

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Must a potential depend only on the ordinary data values, or may it depend on counters maintained by the implementation?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It must be a well-defined function of the analyzed state. The state may include legitimate maintained metadata, so a work counter can be included if its updates and meaning are specified. An arbitrary unrecorded past history is not automatically available to the algorithm. Augmenting the mathematical state can formalize accounting, but the resulting endpoint lower bound and update costs still need proof.

Question 78. Compose two amortized components

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

An operation updates a dynamic array with potential Phi and a queue with potential Psi. Both component bounds use the same real-cost units. Give a combined potential.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Use Ω=Φ+Ψ. If actual cost is the sum of component costs plus a bounded coordination cost, the combined potential difference is the sum of their differences. Thus combined charge is the sum of component charges plus coordination. Retain both initial allowances. If one component move itself calls the other repeatedly, analyze that multiplicity instead of assuming one update each.

Question 79. Operations hidden inside a resize

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A heap insert has logarithmic comparison work and amortized constant array-growth work. What is its amortized total, and can a single insert still be linear?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The components add: comparison work is O(log n) per insert and backing-array work is O(1) amortized, so insertion is O(log n) amortized. A full backing array can force copying n records on a single call, giving linear worst-case time unless the representation is deamortized. Constant growth amortization does not eliminate the heap comparison path.

Question 80. Choose an analysis method

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A process inserts each object once, transfers it at most twice and destroys it once. Transfer costs are respectively two and five, insertion three and destruction four. Derive a total object-work bound.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each object costs at most 3+2+5+4=14 over its lifecycle. For P created objects, aggregate work is at most 14P, plus initial-object work and public-call overhead. An accounting proof could charge fourteen at creation and reserve the remaining eleven. A potential proof could sum pending future obligations. Aggregate counting is simplest because every event already has a fixed lifetime bound.

Question 81. A proof fails at the endpoint

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A potential tends to minus infinity over legal states, but every charge is at most one. Why does this not imply linear total actual work?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Telescoping leaves -ΦN. Without a uniform lower bound or a relative endpoint condition, this term can grow arbitrarily large and pay for arbitrarily much work. For instance define potential as minus cumulative real work in an augmented state: charges can be zero while real work is enormous. Small charges alone are not a complexity theorem.

Question 82. A formula that prices an unused resize

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A student writes copies 1+2+4+8+16 after sixteen appends from capacity one. Correct the expression and explain the strict trigger.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Copies stop at eight: append nine expands from eight to sixteen, but append sixteen only fills the last slot. Copying sixteen belongs to append seventeen. Correct copies are fifteen, and total including sixteen writes is 31. Exact capacity endpoints require testing whether the algorithm grows when old size equals capacity before the append.

Question 83. A symbolic mixed stack bound

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A sequence has P pushes, Q pop calls, R multipop calls, starts with s records and ends with t. Give exact element work if every removal succeeds as far as possible.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Let M be total records removed. Conservation gives M=s+P-t. Element work is P+M=2P+s-t. Public-call overhead one adds P+Q+R. This formula separates requests from actual removals, so a multipop’s requested k need not equal its removed count. The exact endpoint term provides both a bound and a consistency check.

Question 84. Counter operations near a width boundary

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A width-five counter starts at 30 and performs three modulo increments. Count real flips and charges.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Transitions are 11110 to 11111, costing one; 11111 to 00000, costing five; and 00000 to 00001, costing one. Total seven. Charges are two, zero and two, summing four. Initial popcount four and final popcount one give 4+4-1=7. Applying the zero-initial-state formula to this interval would undercount.

Question 85. A shrink gap that vanishes with input

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

Doubling uses shrink threshold β=1/2-1/N. Why can fixed-threshold hysteresis reasoning fail to give a uniform constant?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

After growth occupancy is near one half, only about C/N deletions above beta. When C is on the order of N, only constant many operations can trigger a linear copy. The gap is not a fixed positive constant independent of input. A proof that hides its inverse inside an asymptotic constant cannot claim uniform O(1) amortized cost in N.

Question 86. Zero operations and empty state

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

What are exact work, final capacity and initial clipped potential for zero appends from empty capacity one? Is log zero needed?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Work is zero, capacity remains one and max(0,2n-C) is zero. No logarithm is required. Define the zero case separately before using a positive-input capacity formula. Writing 2⌈log20⌉ is undefined and makes an otherwise correct theorem incomplete at its smallest input.

Question 87. An operation bound is not a mastery guarantee

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original mathematical/conceptual problem or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; no claim of verbatim source reproduction.

A chapter proves correct costs for every legal sequence in its declared model. Does that guarantee a reader will solve every unseen examination question?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. A mathematical theorem has defined assumptions, while unseen questions can use different representations, cost units or operation sets, and successful solving also depends on the reader recognizing those assumptions. The appropriate transfer strategy is to reconstruct the contract, derive the expensive transition and test counterexamples. Verified coverage and worked practice support learning; they cannot prove a universal future-performance statement.

23. Final reasoning rules and examination traps

Final reasoning rules

Rule 1

Distinguish the number of public operations from the current number of stored records; they are different parameters in a sequence theorem.

Rule 2

State the initial structure explicitly, because an arbitrarily preloaded structure can contain unpaid cleanup work.

Rule 3

Identify the charged primitive before computing an exact answer; copied records, comparisons, writes and allocation are different units.

Rule 4

A deterministic amortized theorem applies to every legal sequence and does not require random input order.

Rule 5

Expected time requires an explicit random experiment or distribution; it is not another name for amortized time.

Rule 6

Constant amortized cost permits expensive individual calls, so it does not establish constant latency.

Rule 7

Aggregate analysis counts total real work directly; dividing independent maximum call costs is often unnecessarily pessimistic.

Rule 8

A resource consumed at most once provides a lifetime counting argument only if the operation never recreates that resource without paying again.

Rule 9

Accounting must maintain solvency at every permitted prefix, rather than merely matching totals at the final endpoint.

Rule 10

Credits attached to initial records need an initial allowance; those records were not inserted by the analyzed sequence.

Rule 11

The exact potential identity is actual total equals charge total plus initial potential minus final potential.

Rule 12

Nonnegative potential by itself does not remove a positive initial potential term.

Rule 13

A relative lower bound at least equal to initial potential suffices even if the displayed potential values are negative.

Rule 14

A known global lower bound gives an additive allowance equal to initial potential minus that lower bound.

Rule 15

Negative amortized charges are legal releases of stored credit and must never be interpreted as negative execution time.

Rule 16

Adding a constant to potential changes neither charges nor the difference between its endpoints.

Rule 17

Scaling potential changes the charges and can be necessary when cleanup primitives have higher costs.

Rule 18

Derive a potential coefficient from an exact expensive transition before checking all ordinary transitions.

Rule 19

Big-O and Theta expressions cannot be canceled without bounding their hidden coefficients in the required direction.

Rule 20

A complete case analysis checks both sides of a piecewise potential boundary and the smallest reachable capacity.

Rule 21

A bounded multipop removes the minimum of its requested count and the current size; use actual removals in a cost formula.

Rule 22

Empty multipop has zero element work but still has constant dispatch or check work in a fuller model.

Rule 23

A stack with unit push and unit removal can charge two per push when it starts empty.

Rule 24

A stack with initial size s and final size t has exact element work twice its analyzed pushes plus s minus t.

Rule 25

Multipush changes the input unit: a call creating k records cannot have constant cost independently of k.

Rule 26

An unbounded binary increment flips its trailing ones plus the next zero, and popcount potential gives charge two.

Rule 27

From zero, unbounded binary flips after N increments are exactly twice N minus popcount of N.

Rule 28

The exact counter floor sum includes only bits that exist in the selected representation.

Rule 29

A finite-width all-ones wrap has no new one bit; its bit-flip charge is zero under popcount potential.

Rule 30

A counter beginning nonzero retains its initial popcount in the telescoping formula.

Rule 31

Alternating increment and decrement across a carry boundary defeats the increment-only constant amortized theorem.

Rule 32

A reset that scans every bit can be expensive repeatedly even when the counter is already zero.

Rule 33

Sparse resetting requires maintained metadata or another valid way to reach set positions; it is not a free primitive.

Rule 34

Base-b digit-change potential can use digit sum divided by b minus one, with a fractional charge bound.

Rule 35

Weighted high-bit costs can change constant digit-change amortization to logarithmic average work.

Rule 36

A capacity-one doubling array grows on the append after becoming full, not on the append that fills its last slot.

Rule 37

For positive N, final doubling capacity is the smallest power of two at least N; handle zero separately.

Rule 38

Exact copied records from initial capacity one are final capacity minus one.

Rule 39

Exact copy-plus-write work is N plus final capacity minus one; a linear upper bound is not the exact count.

Rule 40

An initially larger capacity changes the starting term of the geometric copy sum.

Rule 41

Front insertion has shift work that resizing amortization does not remove.

Rule 42

Clipping insert-only potential at zero covers sparse initial states without an artificial negative starting balance.

Rule 43

The doubling growth transition ends after the new record is appended, so its completed potential is two in unit scaling.

Rule 44

A growth factor r gives charge at most one plus r divided by r minus one in the reduced copy/write model.

Rule 45

Integer ceiling preserves the general upper bound but can change the exact growth charge.

Rule 46

A growth factor approaching one with input size does not produce a uniform constant hidden in big-O notation.

Rule 47

Fixed additive capacity growth copies an arithmetic series and yields quadratic total copying.

Rule 48

Allocation or zero-filling a new buffer changes the rebuild coefficient and must be included when the contract charges it.

Rule 49

Nonconstant record constructors or string copies require a cost parameter beyond the number of records.

Rule 50

Pointer invalidation and exception safety are correctness obligations separate from favorable operation counts.

Rule 51

Shrinking at half occupancy after doubling can alternate full-buffer rebuilds on successive insert/delete calls.

Rule 52

Hysteresis requires a strict gap between the occupancy after resize and the opposing trigger.

Rule 53

For growth and shrink factors r, a fixed shrink threshold beta must lie strictly between zero and one divided by r.

Rule 54

A threshold gap that tends to zero with input size can make amortized constants grow with that input.

Rule 55

State whether the quarter-full test occurs before or after removal; exact copies and endpoint potential depend on that timing.

Rule 56

The main post-removal quarter policy uses dense potential twice size minus capacity and sparse potential half capacity minus size.

Rule 57

Crossing from half occupancy into the sparse branch gives a different deletion charge from remaining wholly in the dense branch.

Rule 58

Minimum capacity prevents repeated shrinking below the declared representation boundary and fixes the empty-state contract.

Rule 59

The main minimum-capacity-two policy begins with potential one; retain that one-unit allowance.

Rule 60

Completed-state capacity and peak simultaneous old/new allocation are different space measurements.

Rule 61

A two-stack queue's FIFO order is output from top to bottom followed by input from bottom to top.

Rule 62

Transfer input only when output is empty; moving new records ahead of old output can violate FIFO order.

Rule 63

Twice input size pays for one input pop and one output push per transferred record in the unit stack model.

Rule 64

A transfer-triggered dequeue and a normal output dequeue both have charge one in the primitive-only model.

Rule 65

Total queue size is a poor transfer potential because transferring records hardly changes that size.

Rule 66

A front query can trigger one transfer without removing a record; repeated fronts do not need repeated transfers.

Rule 67

A preloaded input stack supplies initial pending-transfer potential and prevents a from-empty bound from applying unchanged.

Rule 68

In a monotonic stack, each index is pushed once and popped at most once, which bounds total inner-loop iterations.

Rule 69

Failed value comparisons and empty-stack checks are different events and must be counted in the declared model.

Rule 70

Strict-smaller and smaller-or-equal pop rules encode different tie behavior even though both are linear in total.

Rule 71

Sliding-window expiration and dominance remove an index by alternative routes; they do not remove the same stored index twice.

Rule 72

Sorted-block merging costs proportional to output length, whereas a binomial-tree link costs constant primitive work.

Rule 73

Binary-level rebuilding contributes linear work per level across an insertion prefix and therefore logarithmic amortized insertion.

Rule 74

Searching every occupied sorted block can require a quadratic sum in the number of bit levels.

Rule 75

Root-count potential proves a binomial insertion bound only under its specified constant-cost link model.

Rule 76

A competitive move-to-front theorem compares with another algorithm and does not make arbitrary list accesses constant time.

Rule 77

Sparse initialization needs a valid readable-memory contract, round-trip membership checks and an explicit epoch-wrap policy when epochs are used.

Rule 78

Persistent branches can repeat deferred work from the same state; a linear-history potential cannot be spent independently on every branch.

Rule 79

Incremental rebuilding needs an authoritative read/write routing invariant and a deadline before the next capacity exhaustion, plus an allocation assumption.

Rule 80

Transfer learning to unfamiliar questions requires checking representation, costs, initial state, legal operations and triggers; a verified chapter does not imply a guaranteed answer to every unseen question.

24. Editable exact-cost laboratory

Use zero through thirty-two operations, a counter width of two through six and an initial value representable by that width. Sorted-block examples accept at most sixteen insertions. Monotonic input accepts at most twelve integers between minus ninety-nine and ninety-nine. Counter arithmetic wraps at its declared width. Growth charges record copies and writes; allocation is excluded. Monotonic comparisons are shown separately from stack modifications. Large arrays show the first sixteen storage positions and retain the full state in the exact snapshot. Every trace starts paused; invalid input preserves the preceding valid experiment.
